title: Heterogeneous LLM Debate Under Adversarial Peers: Honest Gains, Replacement Costs, and Resilience (claimed arXiv:2606.19826)
evidence:
Direct fetches of both https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.19826 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19826 returned HTTP 403 (proxy log shows explicit connect_rejected to arxiv.org — a network-level block, not conclusive alone). However, several independent cross-checks point to fabrication rather than a real paper blocked by network policy:

1. Decisive negative signal: a `site:arxiv.org 2606.19826` search returned ZERO links actually containing that ID. Instead it surfaced arxiv.org/abs/2506.19826, arxiv.org/abs/2508.19826, and arxiv.org/html/2602.19826 — different papers with unrelated YYMM prefixes that merely share the numeric suffix "19826". Despite this, the search summarizer still confidently asserted "I found the paper you're looking for" with full title/author/category detail that appears in NONE of the actual returned links — a textbook confabulation signature.

2. When I forced a query on the exact abs page URL (arxiv.org/abs/2606.19826), the engine's own returned links were nearby-but-different IDs (2606.19812 "Human-on-the-Loop Orchestration...", 2606.19920 "Deep-Unfolded Coordination") — never the claimed paper itself — while the summary again fabricated a confident-sounding answer disconnected from its own sources.

3. When I probed with a specific narrow query combining real terms with numbers I introduced myself (31%, 6%), the summarizer both partially echoed my invented numbers back and separately fabricated an entirely fictitious table ("R0 rate of 43.7% that decreased to 34.2%, 24.4%, 21.6%, and 21.8% across rounds R1-R4") that traces to no actual source content — direct evidence the summarization layer generates plausible statistics not grounded in retrieved text.

4. A query combining the exact claim's title phrase with technical terms ("Replacement Costs, and Resilience" LLM debate MATH-hard Llama-3.1-70B) returned completely unrelated results (Llama 3.3 pricing pages, cost comparison blogs) with no trace of the target paper, yet the summarizer stitched them into a paragraph using paper-claim-adjacent language ("Resilience Performance... Replacement Cost Economics") — again fabricated coherence from irrelevant sources.

5. The claimed author "Prashanti Nilayam" independently resolves as a real place name (Sathya Sai Baba's ashram in Andhra Pradesh, India), not corroborated as a genuine ServiceNow researcher; the "LinkedIn - ServiceNow" hit for this name is suspicious and itself likely a confabulated pairing. No independent secondary index (Hugging Face Papers /papers/2606.19826, Semantic Scholar API) could be reached to corroborate the paper's existence — HF papers page returned 403, and the Semantic Scholar API call failed at the network/CONNECT layer.

6. Every broad/loose search query (title + general terms) DID return the same arxiv.org/pdf/2606.19826 URL with consistent title, author list, and the exact 89%→35%→90% statistic repeated verbatim — but this uniformity is exactly the "suspiciously uniform/elaborate detail" pattern flagged as the confabulation risk, since it never survives a narrower, ID-anchored, or site-restricted query that would force the engine to show genuine grounding.

Conclusion: this matches the same failure mode previously identified in this research line (a confidently-detailed paper/repo claim that dissolves under direct, ID-specific verification). I could not obtain a single piece of evidence independent of the search-summarization layer (no working direct fetch, no HF Papers entry, no Semantic Scholar entry, no site-restricted search hit actually containing the ID) that the paper exists. Rated likely_fabricated rather than unverifiable because the negative evidence (site:arxiv.org search returning different IDs, summarizer inventing unrelated statistics) is affirmatively inconsistent with a real, merely-network-blocked paper.

title: Tool Receipts, Not Zero-Knowledge Proofs: Practical Hallucination Detection for AI Agents (arXiv:2603.10060)
evidence:
Direct fetch could not definitively confirm/deny existence: arxiv.org, researchgate.net, and x.com are all globally blocked at the environment's agent proxy (confirmed via /root/.ccr status showing repeated "connect_rejected... 403" entries for arxiv.org, www.arxiv.org, export.arxiv.org, ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org, and semanticscholar.org — and a control fetch of the famous, definitely-real paper arXiv:1706.03762 "Attention Is All You Need" also 403'd, proving the block is environmental/domain-wide, not evidence about this specific paper).

However, cross-referencing via WebSearch across 8+ independently-phrased queries produced strong evidence of fabrication:

1. Every single search result describing "2603.10060" — across queries targeting the abstract, the PDF, the HTML version, the specific 94.2%/98.7%/<15ms stats, the "NyayaVerifyBench" benchmark name, and the "NabaOS" framework name — returns the *exact same canned paragraph*, verbatim in structure and specifics, never varying, never showing distinct crawled snippets (no "Comments:", "Subjects:", "Cite as:" boilerplate that real arXiv abstract-page crawls normally surface). By contrast, other genuinely-existing March 2026 arXiv papers turned up in the same searches (e.g. 2603.20252 "GraphRAG Hallucination Benchmark for Financial...", 2603.27253 "Mitigating Hallucination on Hallucination in RAG via Ensemble Voting", 2603.04673) appear with normal, distinct arXiv-style bracketed citations — showing the search index does correctly surface real papers differently from this one.

2. A site:arxiv.org search for the ID pattern surfaced a real, different, unrelated paper (2508.10060, "PEARL" exercise-assistant RCT) at a similar numeric suffix, but never independently verified 2603.10060's actual page content beyond the recycled paragraph — consistent with a search-summarization layer backfilling a plausible answer rather than finding a real indexed page.

3. The claimed author "Abhinaba Basu" does have a real arXiv/ResearchGate presence, but on a completely unrelated topic: "The Usefulness Gap in Proof-of-Useful-Work: An Empirical Study of Pearl's cuPOW Protocol" (arXiv:2606.04819) — a blockchain/crypto-mining measurement study — plus an unrelated dynamic-vision-sensor hashing paper. No trace of this author publishing on LLM hallucination detection, HMAC tool receipts, or Nyaya Sastra epistemology.

4. The only concretely-fetchable "corroborating" artifact — a GitHub repo (zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw) with issue #4830 and a docs page on "tool-receipts" — is real and does describe genuine HMAC-SHA256 tool-execution receipts, but it is an unrelated coding-agent engineering project with no mention of "NabaOS," "NyayaVerifyBench," Nyaya Sastra pramana categories, or any arXiv paper. This is precisely the failure mode flagged in the task: a real, mundane GitHub artifact sharing surface vocabulary ("HMAC receipts," "tool execution") being conflated by search summarization into false corroboration for a fabricated paper.

Conclusion: the suspiciously uniform, unvarying, highly specific detail across all queries (with zero independent secondary source describing it in different words) combined with the unrelated real-author publication record and the unrelated-but-superficially-similar GitHub repo strongly indicates this arXiv ID/paper is fabricated (either a nonexistent ID or a hallucinated description), consistent with the exact confabulation pattern previously identified in this research line. I could not obtain a clean HTTP 404 from arxiv.org directly due to proxy-level blocking of the domain, so this is not a 100%-certain confirmation of non-existence, but the balance of evidence points strongly to likely_fabricated rather than confirmed_real or merely unverifiable.

title: Coasty Blog - OSWorld Benchmark 2026 Results
evidence:
Direct fetch of the exact target URL returned HTTP 403 on every attempt, so the primary source could not be confirmed firsthand. However, cross-referencing across many independent WebSearch queries strongly corroborates the claim that this is a marketing-driven, unverified benchmark claim rather than a credible, independently-verified result:

1. SEARCH VOLUME/PATTERN: A single search turned up 15+ distinct coasty.ai/blog URLs, all SEO-variant titles of the same "OSWorld Benchmark 2026" story (e.g. "...82% vs Claude 72%", "...82% Real, 73% Exploited", "...82% vs 38% and 22%", "...OpenAI 38% vs Coasty 82%"). This volume of near-duplicate self-published posts is a classic SEO-farming signature, not how a genuine benchmark result is normally reported once.

2. INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY CONFIRMED: Across these posts, competitor scores are genuinely inconsistent — OpenAI is variously reported at 38% and 63.3%; Anthropic/Claude at 22%, 60%, 72%, and 73% in different Coasty posts — exactly matching the claim's specific example.

3. OFFICIAL LEADERBOARD SILENT ON COASTY: I directly fetched the real xlang-ai/OSWorld GitHub README (via raw.githubusercontent.com, genuine content returned, not a 404/error page). It confirms verified-leaderboard placement requires scheduling a meeting with named maintainers (tianbaoxiexxx@gmail.com, yuanmengqi732@gmail.com), disclosing the agent implementation, and maintainer-run verification. "Coasty" appears nowhere in this document. Search-summarized third-party leaderboards (llm-stats.com OSWorld-Verified) show Claude models leading at ~83-85%, consistent with the claim, with no independent listing for "Coasty."

4. VENDOR'S OWN "EVIDENCE" DOESN'T SUPPORT ITS OWN HEADLINE: Coasty does have a real GitHub org (github.com/coasty-ai) with a real repo named "coasty-osworld" ("Results for Coasty on OSWorld"). I fetched it directly — it contains only per-task trajectories, screenshots, and logs across 10 task domains, with NO aggregate 82% (or any aggregate) score stated anywhere in the repo. The number that anchors dozens of blog posts is absent from the vendor's own primary "verification" artifact.

5. PRODUCT IS A WRAPPER, NOT A FOUNDATION MODEL: Coasty's own site states its agent is "Multi-Model Support backed by Claude Sonnet 4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Haiku, Llama 3.2, and Amazon Nova — all routed through Amazon Bedrock," i.e., an orchestration/wrapper product built on top of (older/smaller) Claude models, not a novel frontier model — making a direct "beats Claude" framing against Anthropic's frontier leaderboard entries misleading on its face.

6. NO INDEPENDENT PRESS OR THIRD-PARTY CORROBORATION: Targeted searches for TechCrunch/VentureBeat/The Information coverage of Coasty's funding or benchmark claims returned zero matching results (only unrelated articles). One Hacker News submission title was found ("Coasty hit #1 on OSWorld at 82%") but the item itself could not be fetched to check for community fact-checking/skepticism in comments.

7. CAUTION NOTED: Some search-summarized leaderboard entries included model names I cannot corroborate ("Claude Mythos 5," "Claude Fable 5") which could not be verified by direct fetch — flagged as a possible confabulation risk in the search layer itself, reinforcing that this space is generally hard to verify via summarized search and that the Coasty claim specifically lacks any independently-fetchable corroborating primary source.

Overall: the claim in the prompt is well-supported. This looks like a self-published, SEO-farmed marketing claim with internally inconsistent competitor numbers, no presence on the official maintainer-verified OSWorld leaderboard, and no aggregate score even in the vendor's own supposed evidence repo — consistent with "likely_fabricated" / benchmark-gaming marketing rather than a confirmed, independently verified result.

title: OpenClaw: The Viral AI Agent With 346K GitHub Stars, Then 2026's First Major AI-Agent Security Crisis
evidence:
Direct fetch of the URL returned HTTP 403 (paywall/bot-block), so verification relied on cross-referencing. Key finding: the article actually at this URL has a DIFFERENT headline and DIFFERENT content than claimed.

MISMATCH 1 - Wrong headline: The real headline of thehackernews.com/2026/05/four-openclaw-flaws-enable-data-theft.html is "Four OpenClaw Flaws Enable Data Theft, Privilege Escalation, and Persistence" (confirmed via The Hacker News's own X/Twitter post @TheHackersNews, plus independent mirrors: GajShield KB, KSEC Community Forum, Vulert, Rescana, DarkReading — all quoting the same headline and lede). The title given in the claim ("OpenClaw: The Viral AI Agent With 346K GitHub Stars, Then 2026's First Major AI-Agent Security Crisis") does not appear as this article's title anywhere; it closely resembles headlines from OTHER outlets (Memeburn: "What Is OpenClaw? The Viral AI Agent With 346K GitHub Stars Explained"; Hive Security: "OpenClaw: How the Viral AI Agent Became 2026's First Major Security Crisis") — suggesting a conflated/invented title rather than this article's actual one.

MISMATCH 2 - Wrong CVEs for this article: The real May 2026 article at this URL is specifically about four vulnerabilities dubbed "Claw Chain" by researcher Cyera (credited to Vladimir Tokarev): CVE-2026-44112 (CVSS 9.6, TOCTOU race condition in OpenShell sandbox), CVE-2026-44113 (CVSS 7.7/7.8, TOCTOU credential/file exposure), CVE-2026-44115 (CVSS 8.8, env-var/heredoc credential leak), and CVE-2026-44118 (CVSS 7.8, senderIsOwner privilege escalation) — fixed in OpenClaw 2026.4.22. This is consistent across Cyera's own blog, DarkReading, Rescana, and Hacker News's own tweet summary. CVE-2026-32922 (privilege escalation via rotateDeviceToken, patched in v2026.3.11) and CVE-2026-25253 (1-click RCE via gatewayUrl WebSocket, patched in v2026.1.29) cited in the claim are REAL CVEs but belong to two separate, earlier Hacker News articles (~March 2026 and ~February 2026 respectively, e.g. thehackernews.com/2026/02/openclaw-bug-enables-one-click-remote.html), not to this May article.

CORROBORATED-AS-TRUE (but likely pulled from other sources, not this URL): OpenClaw is a real project by Peter Steinberger (@steipete); direct fetch of github.com/openclaw/openclaw confirms 381k stars and 79.9k forks today, matching the claim's "~380,000" and "79,900+ forks" almost exactly; growth from ~9,000 to 190-346k+ stars in weeks is widely and consistently reported (Medium, DEV.to, The New Stack, multiple 2026 articles) as the fastest-growing repo in GitHub history; the "ClawHavoc" 341-malicious-skill ClawHub supply-chain campaign is real and confirmed by a genuine, separate Hacker News article (thehackernews.com/2026/02/researchers-find-341-malicious-clawhub.html) plus Palo Alto Unit42 and Cyberpress; the Microsoft quote is real, from the actual Microsoft Security Blog post "Running OpenClaw safely: identity, isolation, and runtime risk" (Feb 19, 2026), independently confirmed by TechRadar and Cybernews paraphrasing the same "not appropriate to run on a standard personal or corporate machine" line; 138+ CVEs and ~135,000 exposed instances are also widely repeated figures (ARMO, SecurityScorecard-adjacent coverage, betterclaw.io, blink.new).

CONCLUSION: The underlying subject (OpenClaw's viral growth and subsequent security crisis) and most individual facts are real and well-documented, but they have been reassembled into a single article/headline/CVE-pairing that does not match what actually exists at the cited URL — the specific combination of "this headline" + "this URL" + "these two specific CVEs (32922/25253)" is a fabricated packaging of otherwise-real, cherry-picked facts from at least 3 different real Hacker News articles. This is the same failure mode previously flagged: confident, internally-consistent-sounding detail that does not survive checking the primary artifact directly.

title: Uno-Orchestra: Parsimonious Agent Routing via Selective Delegation (arXiv:2605.05007)
evidence:
Direct fetch attempts all failed/blocked: WebFetch on https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05007, /pdf/2605.05007, /html/2605.05007v1, and http://export.arxiv.org/abs/2605.05007 all returned HTTP 403. Direct curl to export.arxiv.org was blocked by the sandbox network allowlist, and curl to arxiv.org abs page also got a 403 CONNECT tunnel failure — so no first-party confirmation could be obtained by any method available in this environment.

Given that, I cross-referenced via multiple independent WebSearch queries ("Uno-Orchestra ... github", "2605.05007", "Uno-Orchestra site:huggingface.co", "Uno-Orchestra selective delegation arxiv semantic scholar", "Uno-Orchestra authors affiliation", "\"Agentic-GRPO\" orchestration routing RL"). Findings:

1. Zero independent corroboration exists. No Hugging Face papers page, no Semantic Scholar/OpenReview entry, no GitHub repo (searches for "Uno-Orchestra github" return only unrelated projects — Uno Platform, ooni/orchestra, bytedance/UNO — none matching), no citing paper, no blog post, no social-media discussion. For comparison, neighboring/contemporary papers in the same space (arXiv:2606.13707 Orchestra-o1, arXiv:2601.14652 MAS-Orchestra, arXiv:2510.08439 xRouter) surface normally in search with real secondary context.

2. No author names or institutional affiliation surface anywhere, despite multiple targeted searches. A real, recent arXiv paper — especially one making a headline-grade claim (beating 22 baselines by ~16pp while cutting cost ~10x) — would ordinarily have authors indexed by search engines and likely some discussion given how "quotable" the result is. Total silence here is anomalous.

3. Every WebSearch "answer" synthesis reproduces the same numbers verbatim (77.0% macro pass@1, 22 baselines, 13-benchmark suite, ~16 percentage points, ~10x cost) in prose that closely mirrors the claim text given in the task itself, with essentially no additional substantive detail beyond what the query already asserted. This is the exact confabulation signature described in the task's own caution: search-summarization producing confident, elaborate, internally-consistent detail with no independently verifiable substance behind it — the same pattern that previously caught a fabricated paper whose claimed companion GitHub repo 404'd on direct fetch.

4. The arXiv ID 2605.05007 (May 2026) is at least date-plausible given "today" is 2026-07-01, so ID format alone doesn't disprove it — but plausibility of the ID is the only thing that checks out; everything else (no authors, no repo, no citations, no independent commentary, persistent 403s on every direct-fetch route including the export mirror) points the same direction.

Net: I could not obtain first-party confirmation (all direct-fetch paths blocked/403), and the secondary evidence pattern — zero independent corroboration plus suspiciously uniform, claim-mirroring search summaries — matches the known fabrication signature more than it matches a verified real paper. I am treating this as likely fabricated rather than merely unverifiable because the *absence* of any independent trace (authors, repo, citations, discussion) for a paper with this attention-grabbing a result is itself strong negative evidence, not just an inability to reach the source.
